storyline.title: Charles IV
storyline.summary: The Luxembourg prince raised in Paris who returned to a ruined castle and rebuilt Prague into an imperial capital.

chapters.name: A Prague childhood, a French education

newEvents.title: Charles IV is born in Prague
newEvents.locationNote: Born in Prague on 14 May 1316 and baptised Wenceslas. The building is not securely identified; Prague Castle had stood damaged and largely unused since the fire of 1303.
newEvents.summary: The eldest son of John of Luxembourg and Elizabeth of Bohemia is born in Prague and baptised Wenceslas.

newEvents.title: Sent to the French court
newEvents.locationNote: Off-map for this storyline: outside the Czech lands. Rendered as a narrative step with no marker until the European chapters are added. He resided at the French court for seven years and took the name Charles at confirmation, after his great-uncle Charles IV of France.
newEvents.summary: Aged seven, he is sent to be raised at the court of Charles IV of France, taking the name Charles at confirmation.

newEvents.title: He returns to a ruined castle
newEvents.locationNote: The state of the castle on his return is described in his own autobiography, the Vita Caroli, which has no standalone English Wikipedia article — cite it directly in the prose rather than leaning on the link. The Prague Castle article confirms only that the royal palace was rebuilt in Gothic style and the fortifications strengthened under his reign. He was still in Lucca at the start of 1333 and reached Bohemia later that year.
newEvents.summary: Returning to Bohemia after a decade abroad, he finds Prague Castle uninhabitable and begins its restoration.

newEvents.title: Prague is raised to an archbishopric
newEvents.locationNote: Elevated on 30 April 1344, ending Prague's status as a suffragan diocese under the archbishopric of Mainz.
newEvents.summary: Prague is freed from the authority of Mainz and made an archbishopric in its own right, the same year the new cathedral is begun.

newEvents.title: Crecy, and his father's death
newEvents.locationNote: Off-map for this storyline: outside the Czech lands. Rendered as a narrative step with no marker until the European chapters are added. Fought 26 August 1346. John, blind, had his horse's bridle tied to those of his attendants and rode into the English line; Charles fought on the French side and was wounded.
newEvents.summary: John of Luxembourg, blind for years, is killed charging the English lines; Charles is wounded and becomes King of Bohemia.

newEvents.title: Crowned King of Bohemia
newEvents.locationNote: Crowned on 2 September 1347. The St Wenceslas Crown was made in 1346, the year before, and dedicated to the patron saint rather than to himself.
newEvents.summary: He is crowned in the still-unfinished cathedral, wearing a new crown made for the occasion and dedicated to St Wenceslas.

newEvents.title: Emmaus Monastery is founded
newEvents.locationNote: The Slavonic-rite detail is not stated outright in the English Wikipedia article, which notes only that students of Cyril and Methodius studied there. The Czech name Na Slovanech supports it; confirm against a better source before asserting it in the prose.
newEvents.summary: A monastery licensed for the Slavonic liturgy is founded in the new district, an unusual concession in a Latin-rite kingdom.

newEvents.title: Karlstejn Castle is founded
newEvents.locationNote: Built to hold the Imperial Regalia, the Bohemian crown jewels and his relic collection, and personally supervised by him during construction.
newEvents.summary: A fortress is begun southwest of Prague to house the imperial regalia and his collection of relics.

newEvents.title: Crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome
newEvents.locationNote: Off-map for this storyline: outside the Czech lands. Rendered as a narrative step with no marker until the European chapters are added. Crowned 5 April 1355, by a cardinal rather than the pope.
newEvents.summary: He is crowned emperor in Rome and leaves the same day, having promised the pope he would not stay.

newEvents.title: The Golden Bull
newEvents.locationNote: Off-map for this storyline: outside the Czech lands. Rendered as a narrative step with no marker until the European chapters are added. Issued in two parts: chapters 1-23 at Nuremberg on 10 January 1356, chapters 24-31 at Metz on 25 December 1356. It named seven prince-electors and set four votes as sufficient to elect a king of the Romans.
newEvents.summary: He fixes the rules for electing a king of the Romans, settling a question that had caused repeated civil war.

newEvents.title: The Hunger Wall on Petrin
newEvents.locationNote: Care needed: the wall's purpose was defensive, and the claim that it was built *in order to* feed the poor is the myth, not the history. What is recorded is that it was first called Zubata (toothed) or Chlebova (built for bread), and that the name Hladova (hungry) took hold after the famine of 1361, when the works did provide a livelihood for the city's poor. The further story that Charles laboured on it himself is legend.
newEvents.summary: A fortification wall is run across the Petrin slope, remembered in tradition as public works built to feed the poor.

newEvents.title: Karlovy Vary is chartered
newEvents.locationNote: Privileges granted 14 August 1370; the settlement itself most likely dates from around 1349. The founding story — that while staying at Loket he led an expedition into the forests, his party found a hot spring by accident, and its water healed his injured leg — is tradition, not record. Coordinates are the town centre, not the springs.
newEvents.summary: The spa town at the hot springs in western Bohemia receives its town privileges and his name.

newEvents.title: He dies at Prague Castle
newEvents.locationNote: Died 29 November 1378, aged 62, and buried at St Vitus Cathedral. The multi-day funeral is widely described but was not confirmed against a source in this pass — verify before asserting the detail.
newEvents.summary: He dies at the castle he had rebuilt, and is buried in the cathedral he had begun.

visitablePlaces.title: His tomb in the royal crypt
The St Wenceslas Crown
visitablePlaces.locationNote: You cannot normally see the original. It is held in a chamber off the St Wenceslas Chapel behind seven locks whose keys are distributed among seven office-holders, and it is brought out roughly once every five years. What visitors see is a replica. Say so plainly — this is the one entry in the collection that could send someone to look at something that is not there.

visitablePlaces.title: His portrait bust in the triforium
visitablePlaces.locationNote: The article confirms the triforium busts depict the royal family, saints, Prague bishops and the two master builders including Parler himself, but does not single out a bust of Charles IV. His is well known; confirm it against a better source before naming it.

visitablePlaces.title: The Chapel of the Holy Cross
Master Theodoric's panel paintings
visitablePlaces.locationName: Karlstejn Castle and the National Gallery Prague
visitablePlaces.locationNote: 129 panels survive of an original 130, in four rows in the Chapel of the Holy Cross. Several are now in the National Gallery Prague rather than at the castle — among them St Luke, St Matthew, St Catherine of Alexandria and St Charlemagne, painted c. 1359-1365. Theodoric was Charles's court painter and is the best-documented Gothic painter in Bohemia.

visitablePlaces.title: The Carolinum
visitablePlaces.locationNote: Do not imply the building dates from the 1348 foundation. Charles donated the property in 1366, and the university did not get proper facilities here until the early 1380s under Wenceslas IV. It is the seat of Charles University today.
